screens.title: Advanced NavMesh Features & Obstacle Avoidance
screens.subtitle: Dynamic obstacles, Off-Mesh Links, manual traversal, and agent tuning

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how Unity extends a baked NavMesh to handle dynamic environments and special movements. We'll look at the NavMeshObstacle component and how its carving behavior temporarily removes walkable area so agents can re-path around moving objects. Then we'll explore Off-Mesh Links, which join two discontinuous points so agents can jump, climb, or teleport across gaps. You will see how disabling automatic link traversal gives you control to play custom animations and precisely move an agent across a link. We will also discuss which NavMeshAgent parameters matter for gameplay and performance, and how to debug common pathing problems using path status and the Navigation debug tools. By the end you will be ready to add a moving obstacle, create an Off-Mesh Link, and implement a manual traversal coroutine that plays a jump arc. Think about a guard that needs to avoid a moving cart and leap over a gap — this chapter shows how to make that feeling believable while keeping performance manageable. Ready to dive into objectives and hands-on steps?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: NavMeshObstacle carves runtime holes; Off-Mesh Links connect discontinuous navigation points; manual traversal enables custom animations and precise control.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: First objective set. You will implement dynamic obstacle avoidance by using the NavMeshObstacle component correctly. That means adding the component to moving scene objects and enabling carve when the object blocks navigation. A concrete example is a door that toggles carve on when closed, forcing agents to re-path. This objective matters because without runtime carving agents will attempt to move through objects that are no longer passable. A common mistake is to add carve to every moving prop, which can be expensive; prefer carve only for persistent, significant obstructions. Second, you will utilize Off-Mesh Links to connect discontinuous walkable areas. You will learn to place links manually or enable automatic generation for expected jumps. For example, two separated platforms become connected by an Off-Mesh Link so an agent can traverse. Understanding this prevents agents from treating valid actions as unreachable. These objectives give you practical skills to make AI navigate complex, changing levels effectively.

screens.title: NavMeshObstacle and Carving
screens.subtitle: How runtime carving changes navigation and when to use it

narration.text: A NavMeshObstacle allows a GameObject to remove a region of the NavMesh at runtime, a process called carving. Practically, carving means the obstacle carves a hole in the walkable surface where it stands, so NavMeshAgents will find alternative routes. For example, a closed door with Carve enabled will make that doorway non-walkable. When the door opens you disable carve so the NavMesh becomes walkable again. Carving supports two shapes, box and capsule, and exposes size and center so you match the obstacle geometry. A common misconception is that every small moving prop should carve; this is unnecessary and can harm performance if many objects are carving each frame. Reserve carving for persistent or blocking objects like doors, crates, or moving elevators. Also prefer toggling the Carve property only when the object actually blocks paths instead of carving continuously. Key practical checks are to ensure the obstacle is on the Navigation layer baked earlier and that its shape matches the physical blocking region. Takeaway: Use NavMeshObstacle carving to make major dynamic blockers behave correctly while minimizing runtime cost. NavMeshObstacle and Carving means use carving for major dynamic blockers; toggle carve to balance accuracy and performance.. In practical terms, how runtime carving changes navigation and when to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NavMeshObstacle takeaway

Definition
NavMeshObstacle lets a GameObject carve out a portion of the NavMesh so agents will avoid that area at runtime.
Shapes & settings
Choose Box or Capsule, set Size and Center, and enable Carve to remove the NavMesh beneath the object.
When to carve
Use carve for persistent, significant dynamic blockers like doors and large crates. Disable carve for small props to save CPU.
Common mistake
Adding carve to all moving objects causes high CPU cost and frequent NavMesh updates.
Key Takeaway

Carve selectively. Toggle Carve during state changes like door close/open to maintain correct paths without continuous cost.

Concrete example
Create a cube with NavMeshObstacle. Add a small script to move it left and right. With Carve enabled the NavMesh recomputes around the cube at runtime and agents will re-path to avoid it.
Debug checks
  • Confirm the obstacle is on the NavMesh layer.
  • Match shape size to the physical collider.
  • Toggle Carve to observe NavMesh holes appear and disappear.
Pro tip
If performance suffers, disable Carve when the obstacle is off-screen or when many obstacles are active; consider alternative avoidance for small props.

screens.title: Off-Mesh Links Explained
screens.subtitle: Connecting discontinuous NavMesh regions for jumps, climbs, and teleports

narration.text: Off-Mesh Links are deliberate connections between two points that are not part of a continuous NavMesh. They let agents perform actions that the baked walkable surface alone cannot represent, such as jumping a gap, climbing a ladder, or using a teleport pad. You can create links manually by placing an Off-Mesh Link object and dragging its start and end to valid NavMesh points. Alternatively, the Navigation bake can auto-generate links for drops and jumps when you enable OffMeshLinkGeneration and set thresholds. A practical example is two small platforms separated by a chasm; an Off-Mesh Link allows your agent to reach the far platform without requiring a continuous bridge. A common misconception is that links teleport agents instantly; by default agents can traverse a link automatically if autoTraverseOffMeshLink is true, which produces a smooth movement. But if you want a jump animation, disable autoTraverse and handle the traversal yourself so you can position and animate the agent precisely. Takeaway: Off-Mesh Links extend the NavMesh model so agents can perform non-walking actions while still following path logic. Off-Mesh Links Explained means off-mesh links join discontinuous navmesh points and can be generated manually or during bake to represent jumps and drops.. In practical terms, connecting discontinuous navmesh regions for jumps, climbs, and teleports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Off-Mesh Links
What is an Off-Mesh Link?
A connection between two NavMesh points that lets agents traverse discontinuous geometry.
Manual placement
Place an Off-Mesh Link object and assign start and end transforms on valid NavMesh positions.
Auto-generation
Enable OffMeshLinkGeneration in the Bake settings to auto-create links for jumps and drops based on parameters.
Common misconception
Off-Mesh Links do not automatically play animations; automatic traversal only handles movement. To play a custom animation you must disable auto traversal and control the movement yourself.
Key Takeaway

Off-Mesh Links let agents perform actions off the baked walkable surface. Use them to model jumps, ladders, and teleports without changing the NavMesh topology.

Concrete scenario
Two isolated platforms separated by a small chasm. Add an Off-Mesh Link between them so an agent heading to a target on the far side can cross without a bridge.
Pro tip
When auto-generating links, inspect endpoints to ensure they lie on suitable NavMesh surfaces; adjust generation thresholds if links are missing or misplaced.

screens.title: Manual Off-Mesh Link Traversal
screens.subtitle: Disable auto traversal and implement a coroutine for custom animation

narration.text: Manual traversal gives you precise control when an agent uses an Off-Mesh Link. The essential steps are: first, set the agent's autoTraverseOffMeshLink property to false so Unity does not move the agent automatically. Second, detect when the agent is on a link by checking its isOnOffMeshLink property. Third, stop the agent from continuing path logic by setting isStopped or using a guard flag. Fourth, access agent. currentOffMeshLinkData to get the link's start and end positions. Fifth, run a coroutine that moves the agent from start to end over time, optionally adding a parabolic offset for a jump arc and triggering animations on an Animator. Sixth, once the manual movement finishes, call agent. CompleteOffMeshLink to return control to NavMeshAgent and resume normal pathfinding. For example, implement a simple coroutine that lerps position while adding sine-based vertical offset to simulate a jump. A common pitfall is forgetting to call CompleteOffMeshLink, which leaves the agent stuck. Takeaway: Manual traversal lets you synchronize visuals, physics, and movement but requires you to manage the agent lifecycle during the traversal. Manual Off-Mesh Link Traversal means disable auto traversal, detect link entry, run a coroutine to move/animate the agent, then call completeoffmeshlink.. In practical terms, disable auto traversal and implement a coroutine for custom animation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Disable auto traversal, detect link entry, run a coroutine to move/animate the agent, then call CompleteOffMeshLink.

screens.title: Understanding the CustomLinkTraversalAI Script
screens.subtitle: Key methods, control flow, and safety checks

narration.text: Let's walk through the CustomLinkTraversalAI script pattern and highlight the parts you must implement carefully. The script obtains a NavMeshAgent reference at Start and applies initial settings like speed and disabling autoTraverseOffMeshLink. The Update method sets the destination while the agent is not traversing a link, guarding with a flag to avoid conflicting control. When the agent isOnOffMeshLink and not already traversing, start a coroutine to handle movement. Inside the coroutine, set isStopped to true or use a guard, read OffMeshLinkData for start and end positions, and perform a timed interpolation while adding a vertical offset for an arc. Use a timer based on jumpDuration, and update transform. position each frame. After finishing, set position to the end point, call agent. CompleteOffMeshLink to inform the NavMesh system, and re-enable agent movement. The script also demonstrates using an Animator if present, but avoid depending on an animator to prevent null-reference errors. A common error is moving the agent by setting NavMeshAgent next position directly instead of transform during manual control; choose the approach consistent with your physics and root motion setup. Takeaway: implement guards, call CompleteOffMeshLink, and reset state to avoid stuck agents.

keyIdea.title: Script highlights
keyIdea.text: Check references, guard coroutines, move transform with an arc, then call CompleteOffMeshLink and resume the agent.

screens.title: Auto vs Manual Off-Mesh Traversal
screens.subtitle: When to let the agent move automatically and when to take control

narration.text: Choosing between automatic Off-Mesh Link traversal and manual control depends on the behavior you need. Automatic traversal is simple: set autoTraverseOffMeshLink to true and the NavMeshAgent will move across links smoothly using its pathing logic. This is efficient and works well for small or invisible transitions where no special animation is required. Manual traversal is appropriate when you need to play a jump or climbing animation, synchronize root motion, or perform precise movement such as climbing a ladder with an eye-catching pose. To implement manual control, disable autoTraverse and handle isOnOffMeshLink in code, moving the agent and calling CompleteOffMeshLink when done. An important practical contrast: automatic traversal is lower-cost and reduces code complexity, but it cannot play your custom animation or adjust timing. Manual control increases fidelity but requires you to manage agent stopping, movement interpolation, animation events, and calling CompleteOffMeshLink. A common mistake is leaving autoTraverse enabled and attempting manual animation at the same time; this conflicts and produces unpredictable motion. Takeaway: default to automatic traversal for simple movement and use manual traversal when visual accuracy or animation timing matters.

keyIdea.title: Auto vs Manual
keyIdea.text: Auto traversal is simple and efficient; manual traversal is needed for custom animations and precise control.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Auto vs Manual Traversal
Auto traversal
Pros: simple, low code, smooth movement. Cons: cannot play custom animations or control timing.
When to use
Small transitions or when visual fidelity is not required.
Misuse to avoid
Don't enable autoTraverse if you intend to animate the agent manually; they will fight for control.
Manual traversal
Pros: full control over animation and timing. Cons: more code and responsibility to resume pathing correctly.
When to use
When you need a jump, climb, or landing animation synchronized with movement.
Key Takeaway

Pick automatic for low-friction movement and manual for animation fidelity; never mix both at once for the same traversal.

screens.title: Agent Parameters & Performance
screens.subtitle: Which NavMeshAgent properties affect behavior and CPU cost

narration.text: NavMeshAgent exposes several parameters that control movement and local avoidance. The most impactful for gameplay are speed, acceleration, stoppingDistance, radius, and Obstacle Avoidance Type. Speed and acceleration influence how fast and responsively an agent reaches its destination. stoppingDistance controls how close the agent comes to its target before stopping, useful for cover or maintaining spacing. The radius governs runtime collision for local avoidance and differs from the baked agent radius: changing runtime radius affects how agents negotiate local obstacles and each other. Obstacle Avoidance Type selects between None, Low, Medium, and High quality avoidance—which trades C P U for smoother avoidance. On scenes with many agents, lowering avoidance quality or disabling it for background agents reduces C P U pressure. A typical pattern is to use high-quality avoidance for player-facing enemies and lower settings for distant or non-critical agents. Always test with representative agent counts. Misconception to avoid: assuming bake-time agent radius is the only setting that matters at runtime. The agent's runtime radius and avoidance settings determine local steering behavior. Takeaway: tune parameters per AI role and validate performance with profiling or simplified agent counts.

keyIdea.title: Tuning takeaway
keyIdea.text: Tune speed, radius, stopping distance, and avoidance quality per agent role; lower avoidance for background agents to save CPU.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Agent Parameters
Key properties
Speed & Acceleration
Control movement responsiveness and maximum walk speed.
Stopping Distance
How close the agent gets before it stops, useful for cover or formation spacing.
Radius (runtime)
Defines local avoidance collision size; affects how agents steer around each other.
Avoidance & Performance
Obstacle Avoidance Type trades CPU for quality. Use high quality for a small number of agents near the player, and lower quality for many background agents.
Practical strategy
Categorize AI by role and assign avoidance quality accordingly. Profile with realistic agent counts to confirm performance impact.
Misconception
Do not assume baked agent radius solves runtime steering; adjust runtime radius and avoidance settings for desired behavior.

screens.title: Debugging Advanced NavMesh Issues
screens.subtitle: Use pathStatus and Navigation debug tools to find problems

narration.text: Debugging navigation issues requires tools and a methodical approach. The agent. pathStatus property is your first clue: a Complete status means the agent has a full path, Partial means it could not reach the exact destination, and Invalid indicates no path was found. When you see Partial, check for unreachable endpoints, Off-Mesh Links misplacement, or carving that removed necessary NavMesh areas. Use the Navigation window and enable the debug views for Areas and Obstacles to visualize the baked NavMesh and runtime carvings. Inspect Off-Mesh Link endpoints to ensure they sit on valid NavMesh polygons. In the Scene view you can also draw the agent's path corners via Gizmos to see where pathfinding stops. A common oversight is not verifying the agent's layer or the NavMesh bake settings: ensure the agent's size and allowed areas were baked using appropriate bake parameters. Another check is to reduce agent avoidance quality temporarily to see if avoidance logic is blocking movement. Takeaway: combine agent. pathStatus checks with the Navigation debug views and path gizmos to quickly locate whether the issue is path availability, link placement, or runtime carving.

keyIdea.title: Debugging takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use pathStatus, Navigation debug views, and path gizmos together to identify whether issues come from baking, links, or runtime carving.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Debugging NavMesh
Path status meanings
  • Complete: Full path to destination.
  • Partial: Reached closest reachable point; destination unreachable.
  • Invalid: No path computed.
Checks to run
  1. Open Navigation debug and inspect Areas and Obstacles.
  2. Verify Off-Mesh Link endpoints lie on NavMesh polygons.
  3. See if runtime carving removed needed NavMesh polygons.
Scene debugging aids
Use an OnDrawGizmos method to draw agent.path.corners lines and spheres at each corner to visualize the found path and where it stops. Toggle obstacle carve to watch NavMesh holes appear and disappear.
Key Takeaway

Combine programmatic pathStatus checks with the Navigation debug view and path gizmos to find whether the problem is bake-time or runtime behavior.

screens.title: Hands-on: Moving Obstacle and Off-Mesh Jump
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step lab to observe carving and manual traversal

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through implementing a moving obstacle with carving and a manual Off-Mesh Link jump. Start with a scene that already has a baked NavMesh. Add a 3D cube and give it a NavMeshObstacle component; enable Carve. Add a simple script to move the cube left and right using a sine function so it crosses potential agent paths. Next, create two platforms separated by a chasm and add an Off-Mesh Link between them, placing start and end points on valid NavMesh surfaces. Create a NavMeshAgent character and assign a target on the far platform. In the agent script set autoTraverseOffMeshLink to false. In Update, if agent. isOnOffMeshLink and not already traversing, start a coroutine that stops the agent, reads the link start and end, lerps the transform with a parabolic offset over the desired jumpDuration, sets transform to end, calls agent. CompleteOffMeshLink, and resumes movement. Run the scene and observe the agent re-pathing around the moving cube and performing the jump. If the agent gets stuck, check that CompleteOffMeshLink is called and that the Off-Mesh Link endpoints are on walkable NavMesh areas. This lab makes the interaction tangible and prepares you for tuning.

keyIdea.text: A moving carved obstacle forces re-pathing while an agent performs a manual jump across an Off-Mesh Link using a coroutine.

screens.title: Performance Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: How to avoid high-cost NavMesh operations and keep AI responsive

narration.text: When implementing dynamic navigation, several common mistakes repeatedly cause performance or behavior problems. First, enabling Carve on many small moving objects makes Unity recompute NavMesh regions repeatedly, which can spike C P U usage. Best practice: carve only for objects that meaningfully block navigation and enable carve only when the object is actively blocking. Second, using high-quality obstacle avoidance for vast numbers of agents leads to heavy steering computation. Instead categorize agents and lower avoidance quality or disable it for background units. Third, forgetting to call agent. CompleteOffMeshLink after manual traversal leaves agents in a stuck state; always complete the link and resume agent movement. Fourth, misplacing Off-Mesh Link endpoints off the NavMesh produces Partial paths. Always verify endpoints lie on valid NavMesh polygons using the Navigation debug view. Finally, mixing automatic traversal with manual animation causes control conflicts; choose one approach per link. The overall best practice is to balance visual fidelity with C P U budget, test with realistic agent counts, and use toggles or role-based settings to optimize both gameplay and performance. Performance Pitfalls and Best Practices means selective carving, role-based avoidance settings, and careful link placement are essential to maintain performance and correct behavior.. In practical terms, how to avoid high-cost navmesh operations and keep ai responsive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Performance summary
keyIdea.text: Selective carving, role-based avoidance settings, and careful link placement are essential to maintain performance and correct behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Performance Pitfalls
Pitfall: Excessive carving
Carving many objects every frame causes frequent NavMesh updates. Use carve sparingly and toggle it when needed.
Pitfall: High avoidance on all agents
High-quality avoidance scales poorly. Assign quality by importance and test with realistic counts.
Pitfall: Missing CompleteOffMeshLink
Forgetting to call it after manual traversal prevents the agent from resuming normal pathfinding.
Pitfall: Bad link placement
Ensure endpoints lie on valid NavMesh areas; otherwise pathfinding will report Partial or Invalid.
Key Takeaway

Design with role-based settings and selective carving to balance fidelity and performance. Test under realistic conditions.

screens.title: Live-coding: Implementing the Jump Coroutine
screens.subtitle: Practical code sample and testing tips for a parabolic jump

narration.text: In this demo-style explanation we focus on the jump coroutine you will write for manual Off-Mesh Link traversal. Start by storing OffMeshLinkData and extracting start and end positions. Record the agent transform position and optionally set isStopped or a guard flag to prevent movement. Use a timer loop based on a jumpDuration value and compute normalized time t as timer divided by jumpDuration. Compute the current position by linearly interpolating between start and end, then add a vertical offset using a sine function times jumpHeight to form a parabola. Each frame set transform. position to the computed value and yield until the duration completes. After the loop, snap transform. position to end and call agent. CompleteOffMeshLink, then clear the guard so normal pathing resumes. Test tips: start with a visible arc using a larger jumpHeight and shorter duration to confirm movement, then tune values to match animation speed if you have one. Also verify that you set the agent speed and animator parameters outside the coroutine so walking animation transitions are consistent. Takeaway: the coroutine approach is straightforward and flexible — tune timing and height to match your game's visual needs.

keyIdea.title: Jump coroutine summary
keyIdea.text: Lerp start to end over jumpDuration, add sine-based vertical offset, snap to end, call CompleteOffMeshLink, then resume agent.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three core concepts to keep in mind. First, the NavMeshObstacle component carves runtime holes in the NavMesh when Carve is enabled; use this for significant, persistent blockers and toggle Carve only when necessary to limit C P U cost. Second, Off-Mesh Links connect non-contiguous NavMesh areas so agents can jump, climb, or teleport; ensure endpoints sit on valid NavMesh polygons and choose manual traversal when you need custom animation. Third, autoTraverseOffMeshLink gives a fast, low-code traversal path, while disabling it hands control to your script; if you take manual control remember to call CompleteOffMeshLink after your animation or movement. These three ideas form the foundation for making agents navigate changing environments while still behaving believably. Keep them as design rules while implementing dynamic obstacles and special movement behaviors.

keyIdea.title: Summary strip
keyIdea.text: Carving, links, and traversal control are the core mechanisms for dynamic navigation and believable agent movement.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Key Concepts
NavMeshObstacle

Connects two non-walkable points so agents can jump or climb.
Traversal Control
Use autoTraverse for simple moves; disable it to run custom animation and call CompleteOffMeshLink.
Takeaway
Combine selective carving with link placement and controlled traversal to build believable, scalable navigation behaviors.
